body:
What is hydropower?

Hydropower is power obtained from the energy of moving or falling water. When this energy is used to turn a turbine connected to an electrical generator, the electricity produced is called hydroelectricity.

Hydropower is generally classified as renewable because the water supplying rivers and reservoirs is replenished through the natural water cycle. However, the amount of water available at a particular place can change substantially from one season or year to another.

Connection with the water cycle

Solar heating causes water to evaporate from oceans, lakes and land. Water vapour later condenses and returns to the surface as precipitation. Rainfall and snowmelt feed streams and rivers, while terrain allows water to flow from higher elevations towards lower elevations.

Hydropower plants use this movement of water. Their operation therefore depends on both water availability and the difference in elevation through which the water moves.

Head and water discharge

Two basic quantities help explain the energy available to a hydropower plant.

  • Head: The vertical difference in water level available to drive the turbine. In simple terms, it represents the useful drop in height through which water can release energy.
  • Discharge: The volume of water flowing through a point in a given time, commonly expressed in cubic metres per second.

Other conditions being similar, a greater head or a greater discharge can allow more power to be generated. A steep mountain stream may provide useful head with comparatively little water, whereas a broad river may support generation using a larger flow and a smaller head.

Hydropower depends on both head and flow. A large volume of water without a useful elevation difference, or a large elevation difference without sufficient water, may not provide the desired generation.

How a conventional hydroelectric plant works

  1. Water availability: Water is available in a reservoir or flowing river at a suitable elevation.
  2. Intake: Water enters the power-generating route through an intake structure.
  3. Conveyance: Water travels through a canal, tunnel or penstock, which is a closed pipe carrying water towards the turbine.
  4. Turbine rotation: Water passes through the turbine and transfers part of its energy to the rotating blades or runner.
  5. Electricity generation: The rotating turbine drives a generator that produces electricity.
  6. Return to the river: Water leaves the powerhouse through a downstream channel or tailrace.

The energy conversion is gravitational potential energy of elevated water → kinetic energy of moving water → mechanical energy of the turbine → electrical energy.

Hydropower does not require burning coal, petroleum or natural gas at the generating plant. The water that passes through the turbine is not chemically consumed in generating electricity. Nevertheless, reservoirs may lose water through evaporation or seepage, and water withdrawals for other purposes may reduce the amount available for generation.

Is a dam always necessary?

No. Many hydropower plants use dams and reservoirs, but some use natural river gradients with diversion channels, small barriers or penstocks. A large reservoir is therefore not a defining requirement for all hydropower systems.

Mountainous regions are often suitable because their steep gradients can provide useful head. Rivers with substantial flow can also support hydropower through appropriately selected arrangements. Hydropower potential must be assessed using actual river conditions rather than the mere presence of water.

Basic components and their functions

ComponentMain purpose
DamObstructs or regulates river flow and may form a reservoir.
ReservoirStores water for later use where storage is provided.
IntakeDirects water into the generating route.
PenstockConveys water towards the turbine.
TurbineConverts water energy into mechanical rotation.
GeneratorConverts mechanical rotation into electricity.
TailraceReturns water to the downstream watercourse.
SpillwayAllows controlled passage of water outside the generating route when required.

A spillway is primarily associated with water release and dam safety. It should not be confused with a penstock, which carries water towards a turbine for generation.

Prelims focus

  • Hydroelectricity is generated by using the energy of moving water to drive a turbine and generator.
  • Head is the useful difference in elevation; discharge is the volume flowing per unit time.
  • A penstock carries water to the turbine, while a tailrace returns it downstream.
  • A spillway is used for water release and safety, not as the normal energy-conversion component.
  • Hydropower is connected to the naturally replenished water cycle.
  • Trap: Not every hydropower plant requires a large dam or reservoir.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8 Geography, Chapter 3, Mineral and Power Resources, 2018–19 edition, pp. 32–33 and Figure 3.14; NCERT, Science, Class 10, Chapter 14, Sources of Energy, hydropower discussion; U.S. Department of Energy, How Hydropower Works?, sections How Do We Get Energy from Water? and How Exactly Is Electricity Generated at Hydropower Plants?; U.S. Department of Energy, Types of Hydropower Plants, sections Impoundment and Diversion; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Hydropower: Energy from Flowing Water and the Hydroelectric Generation Process

body:
Why hydropower plants have different operating patterns

Hydropower systems use the energy of moving water, but they differ in how water is supplied and controlled. The most important introductory distinction is between run-of-river, reservoir-based storage and pumped-storage hydropower.

These categories are based on the way water is managed. They should not be confused with the separate classification of hydropower projects by installed generating capacity.

Run-of-river hydropower

A run-of-river plant primarily uses water arriving naturally in a river. The water may be diverted through a channel or penstock to a turbine before returning downstream.

A run-of-river project may use a small dam or weir to direct water. What distinguishes it from a large storage project is that it generally has little or no capacity to store large quantities of water for later seasonal use.

With little storage, electricity production follows changes in river flow relatively closely. Generation may be higher when river discharge is high and lower during dry periods. This arrangement may avoid the extensive submergence associated with a large reservoir, although diversion structures can still alter river habitats.

Run-of-river with pondage

Some run-of-river projects have pondage, meaning limited short-term water storage. This can allow water to be held for part of a day and released when electricity demand is higher.

Run-of-river without pondage has little ability to shift generation in time, whereas run-of-river with pondage can provide limited daily regulation. Pondage is not equivalent to storing large seasonal inflows in a major reservoir.

Reservoir or storage hydropower

A storage hydropower project uses a reservoir to retain water and release it when needed. A dam may store part of the water received during a rainy season so that it can be used during a later period.

Stored water gives greater control over the timing of electricity generation. It can also support irrigation, drinking-water supply and other purposes. However, generating flexibility depends on the water actually available, reservoir conditions and obligations towards other water users and downstream ecosystems.

Reservoir storage does not create additional water. A prolonged drought can reduce generation even at a large dam. During heavy rainfall, safe reservoir management may require releasing water regardless of electricity demand.

Pumped-storage hydropower

Pumped-storage hydropower is primarily a means of storing energy. It uses 2 reservoirs at different elevations.

  1. Charging or pumping: Electricity is used to pump water from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir.
  2. Energy storage: The raised water possesses gravitational potential energy because of its height.
  3. Discharging or generating: When electricity is needed, water flows from the upper reservoir through a turbine to the lower reservoir and drives a generator.

Pumped storage is particularly useful for using electricity available during periods of lower demand or renewable-energy surplus and supplying electricity during periods of greater demand. It can help manage variable wind and solar generation.

Pumped storage does not create net energy

Pumping consumes electricity. Because energy is lost during pumping, water movement and generation, the electricity recovered during a complete pumping-and-generating cycle is less than the electricity used for pumping. Its value is the ability to store energy and deliver it at another time, not to produce extra energy from nothing.

Some pumped-storage schemes have a connection to a natural river or other water body, while others largely circulate water between reservoirs. Where a project also receives natural inflow, that inflow must be distinguished from the energy-storage function of pumping.

Comparison of hydropower arrangements

ArrangementWater managementGeneration patternMain distinction
Run-of-river without pondageLittle or no storage.Closely follows incoming river flow.Limited control over timing.
Run-of-river with pondageSmall short-term storage.Can shift some generation within a day.Limited daily regulation.
Reservoir storageWater retained in a reservoir.Releases can be regulated within water limits.Can store water across longer periods.
Pumped storageWater pumped between 2 elevations.Consumes electricity while pumping and generates during discharge.Stores previously supplied energy.

Small hydropower and mini-hydel applications

Small hydropower projects can supply electricity to villages, remote settlements, local facilities or larger electricity networks, depending on their size and arrangement. In mountainous areas, streams with dependable flow and useful head may support small or mini-hydel generation.

The Government of India's Ministry of New and Renewable Energy uses 1 MW to 25 MW, inclusive, as the eligible installed-capacity range for the Small Hydro Power Development Scheme for financial years 2026–27 to 2030–31. This is the scope of that scheme as issued in 2026; smaller systems can exist outside its eligibility range, and definitions differ between countries.

The capacity classification does not determine the water-management arrangement. A relatively small hydropower project may be run-of-river, while storage and pumped-storage describe different ways of managing water and energy.

Prelims focus

  • Run-of-river plants depend mainly on incoming river flow and may operate without a large reservoir.
  • Pondage provides limited short-term storage; it is not the same as seasonal reservoir storage.
  • Reservoir hydropower can regulate water release, subject to water availability and other obligations.
  • Pumped storage uses 2 reservoirs at different elevations and requires electricity for pumping.
  • MNRE's 2026–27 to 2030–31 Small Hydro Power Development Scheme covers projects from 1 MW to 25 MW, inclusive.
  • Trap: Pumped storage is an energy-storage method; pumping itself does not generate additional net electricity.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Types of Hydropower Plants, sections Impoundment, Diversion and Pumped Storage; U.S. Department of Energy, Pumped Storage Hydropower, section What Is Pumped Storage Hydropower?; Central Electricity Authority and Danish Energy Agency, Indian Technology Catalogue: Generation and Storage of Electricity, January 2022, hydropower section; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Small Hydro Power Development Scheme Guidelines, 2026, Section 1.2; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11 Economics, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, p. 174, Mini-hydel Plants; online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Pumped storage moves water upward using electricity and releases it downward to generate electricity later.

title: Run-of-River, Storage and Pumped-Storage Hydropower: How They Differ

body:
Why some dams are called multipurpose projects

A multipurpose river-valley project is designed to serve more than one water-related purpose. A reservoir may support electricity generation while also supplying irrigation water, drinking water and water for industries.

Water stored behind a dam can be directed to different uses through canals, pipelines, powerhouses and controlled releases. These benefits are related but not identical: water released through a turbine produces electricity, while water supplied to farms provides irrigation. The same reservoir may serve both purposes at different times or through different routes.

Main benefits of multipurpose reservoirs

  • Hydroelectricity: Water released through turbines generates electricity.
  • Irrigation: Stored water can supply agricultural land, including during periods of insufficient rainfall.
  • Drinking and industrial water: Reservoirs can provide managed water supplies to settlements and industries.
  • Flood moderation: Available reservoir space can temporarily retain part of a flood inflow and allow more controlled releases.
  • Other uses: Depending on the project, reservoirs may support fisheries, recreation and related activities.

A project described as multipurpose need not provide every benefit in this list. Its actual functions depend on its design, location and operating arrangements.

Flood control is not an absolute guarantee

Reservoirs can moderate some floods by retaining part of the incoming water. This requires suitable operating conditions, particularly adequate available storage space.

If a reservoir is already near its permitted maximum level or incoming floodwater exceeds the volume that can safely be stored, additional water may have to be released. Flood moderation therefore depends on rainfall and river forecasts, reservoir operation and safe discharge arrangements.

There can be competing demands. Keeping a reservoir relatively full may benefit irrigation and later water supply, while leaving sufficient space may help accommodate a future flood. A multipurpose project must manage these demands together.

Sardar Sarovar Project on the Narmada

The Sardar Sarovar Project is a major multipurpose project on the Narmada River in Gujarat. It combines a dam and reservoir with hydropower facilities and an extensive canal-based water-supply and irrigation system.

The project demonstrates how a major river-valley scheme may provide electricity while also directing water to agricultural and domestic uses. Its benefits extend beyond the location of the dam through the distribution of water to other areas.

Sardar Sarovar hydropower capacity

The Government of Gujarat's Water Scenario and Vision Plan of Gujarat State, Section 1.6.1, lists 1,450 MW of installed hydropower capacity for the Sardar Sarovar Project. This is the installed-capacity figure in the consulted government project profile, not a statement that the project continuously generates 1,450 MW or produces that amount of energy every hour.

The project is also closely associated with questions of environmental protection, displacement and rehabilitation. These concerns form part of understanding multipurpose development rather than being separate from it.

Ukai Project on the Tapi

The Ukai Dam, also called Vallabh Sagar, is situated on the Tapi River in Gujarat. It is another example of a multipurpose reservoir associated with irrigation, hydropower generation and flood moderation.

The Central Water Commission examined sedimentation in the Ukai reservoir in its September 2021 study using satellite data from 2019–2020. The study illustrates an important operational problem: sediment deposited in a reservoir can gradually reduce the space available for water storage.

The Ukai example also shows why a large hydropower project cannot be understood only as a generating station. Reservoir management has consequences for downstream river flow, agriculture, flood conditions and other water users.

How benefits can reach areas beyond the dam

Water released from a reservoir may move through a canal network to fields or settlements far from the dam. A project can therefore contribute to agriculture in areas where local rainfall alone is inadequate.

However, increased irrigation does not automatically eliminate water-management problems. Waterlogging, salinity, unequal access and excessive water demand can arise if irrigation is poorly managed.

Multipurpose benefits require balanced management

Electricity generation, irrigation, flood management and ecological protection may require different patterns of water release. For example, releasing large volumes to maximise electricity generation at one moment may not match the timing of downstream irrigation requirements or environmental-flow needs.

The important principle is that multipurpose development joins several objectives within one river system. Decisions about one use of the water can affect the others.

Prelims focus

  • Multipurpose dams may combine hydropower, irrigation, water supply and flood moderation.
  • Sardar Sarovar is a multipurpose project on the Narmada River in Gujarat.
  • The consulted Gujarat government project profile lists Sardar Sarovar's installed hydropower capacity as 1,450 MW.
  • Ukai Dam is on the Tapi River in Gujarat and serves irrigation, power generation and flood-control purposes.
  • Reservoir sedimentation can reduce useful water-storage capacity.
  • Trap: A dam can reduce some flood peaks, but it cannot guarantee the prevention of every downstream flood.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary India–II, Class 10 Geography, Chapter 3, Water Resources, pp. 26–29; Government of Gujarat, Water Scenario and Vision Plan of Gujarat State, Chapter 1, Sections 1.6 and 1.6.1, consulted 16 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Final Raising of Sardar Sarovar Dam Cleared by Narmada Control Authority, 2017; Central Water Commission, Sedimentation Assessment of Ukai Reservoir, Gujarat, Through Satellite Remote Sensing, September 2021, executive summary and Study Area section, using 2019–2020 satellite data; U.S. Department of Energy, Types of Hydropower Plants, Impoundment section, consulted 16 November 2026.]
